channel.title: Applying biplotEZ
channel.description: Showcasing how the biplotEZ R package is applied to interesting data sets.

item.title: What makes a gut microbiome sample unusual?
item.dc:creator: Raeesa
item.description:
The data

In a study of the gut microbiome and colorectal cancer, Nakatsu et al. (2015) collected bacterial counts from tissue samples. The data considered here contain counts for six bacterial groups: Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Fusobacteria, Actinobacteria, and a sixth category combining all remaining bacteria.

Two subsets of the data are looked at: 61 samples from healthy individuals and 52 samples taken from tissue adjacent to tumours in patients with colorectal cancer.

Van Heerden et al. (2026) recently proposed a statistical model for identifying unusual observations in microbiome count data. Their approach distinguishes between typical samples and samples that exhibit considerably more variation. When applied to these data, the model identifies 11 unusual samples in the healthy group and 7 in the cancer group.

This gives a useful starting point, but it also raises an interesting question.

What makes these samples unusual?

The model identifies observations that differ from the rest, but it is less obvious what makes them different. Are certain bacterial groups responsible? Do the unusual samples share similar characteristics, or are they unusual for different reasons?

This is where a PCA biplot can be useful. Rather than simply identifying unusual samples, we can explore their positions relative to the other observations and see how these relate to the bacterial groups.

Constructing the biplots

Before applying PCA, we need to account for the nature of the data. Bacterial counts depend on the total number of reads in a sample, so comparing raw counts can be misleading. It is of more interest to use the relative abundance of the bacterial groups.

To do this, a centred log-ratio (CLR) transformation is applied, adding a pseudo-count of 0.5 beforehand to accommodate zero counts.

There is also a small but important decision in how the biplots are constructed.

Rather than fitting PCA to all the samples, we use only those classified as typical by the model. The unusual samples are then projected onto the resulting biplot. This means that the unusual observations do not influence the principal components, allowing to see where they fall relative to the structure of the typical samples.

Finally, a ring around each point is drawn. The model gives each sample a probability of being typical, and it classifies a sample as unusual when this probability is 0.5 or less. The ring shows how near that probability is to 0.5: the nearer it is, the larger the ring. A large ring therefore marks a sample that the model is not sure about, while a point with no visible ring is one where the model is confident.

Show the R code 
library(CDM)        # the model and the data
library(biplotEZ)   # development version, draws with ggplot2
library(ggplot2)

# Centred log-ratio. The pseudo-count removes zeros.
clr <- function(Y, pseudo = 0.5) {
  L <- log(Y + pseudo)
  L - rowMeans(L)
}

cdm_biplot <- function(Y, title) {
  Y <- as.matrix(Y)
  storage.mode(Y) <- "integer"

  # Fit the model. A sample is unusual if P(typical) is 0.5 or less.
  fit <- CDM.fit(Y)
  post <- fit$Probability.Posterior[, 1]
  unusual <- post <= 0.5

  Z <- clr(Y)
  rownames(Z) <- seq_len(nrow(Z))

  # Typical samples set the axes. Unusual samples are added afterwards.
  bp <- biplot(Z[!unusual, , drop = FALSE], Title = title) |>
    PCA() |>
    samples(col = "darkorange", pch = 16) |>
    axes(col = "grey40") |>
    interpolate(newdata = Z[unusual, , drop = FALSE]) |>
    newsamples(col = "dodgerblue3", pch = 15, cex = 1.3, label = TRUE)

  # Doubt: 0 = the model is sure, 1 = P(typical) is 0.5
  scores <- rbind(bp$Z, bp$Znew)
  ord <- c(which(!unusual), which(unusual))
  rings <- data.frame(x = scores[, 1], y = scores[, 2],
                       doubt = 1 - 2 * abs(post[ord] - 0.5))

  gg_biplot(bp, draw = FALSE,
            xlim = range(scores[, 1]) * 1.2,
            ylim = range(scores[, 2]) * 1.2)$gg +
    geom_point(data = rings, aes(x = x, y = y), inherit.aes = FALSE,
               shape = 1, colour = "grey30", size = 2.2 + 8 * rings$doubt)
}
Show the R code 
data("Healthy_Subset")
cdm_biplot(Healthy_Subset, "Healthy samples")
Show the R code 
data("Carcinoma_Subset")
cdm_biplot(Carcinoma_Subset, "Samples next to a tumour")

What can we see?

In each biplot, the points represent tissue samples and the axes represent bacterial groups. The tick marks are on the log-ratio scale, and a sample can be projected onto an axis to get an indication of its value for that bacterial group.

The first thing that stands out is the position of the unusual samples. In both biplots, most of the blue squares fall towards the edges of the orange point cloud, or beyond it.

This is reassuring, since the PCA was constructed using only the typical samples. The visual separation is broadly consistent with the classifications produced by the model.

The first two principal components account for approximately 82% of the variation among the typical healthy samples and 73% among the typical cancer samples. Therefore a substantial proportion of the variation can be retained in these two-dimensional displays.

Healthy samples: the role of Proteobacteria

In the healthy samples, the unusual observations are not scattered randomly around the typical samples. Most appear on the side of the biplot associated with higher relative abundances of Proteobacteria, with three samples lying particularly far in this direction.

The widest spread of the samples runs along the Fusobacteria axis. Fusobacteria is absent from 14 of the 61 healthy samples, and the difference between samples with and without this group explains more than half of that spread.

Although Fusobacteria contributes strongly to the overall structure of the biplot, Proteobacteria appears to be more useful for understanding why several of the healthy samples were classified as unusual.

Cancer samples: the role of Fusobacteria

The picture is somewhat different for the cancer samples.

Here, the unusual observations tend to lie at opposite ends of the Fusobacteria axis. Three samples have particularly high relative abundances of Fusobacteria, while two have particularly low relative abundances.

What is particularly useful here is that the unusual samples are not all unusual in the same direction. Some have much higher relative abundances, while others have much lower relative abundances.

The biplot makes this distinction immediately visible.

Some thoughts

What I like about this example is how the statistical model and the biplots complement each other.

The model provides a principled way of identifying unusual samples. The biplots then help us understand what distinguishes those samples from the rest.

For the healthy samples, Proteobacteria appears to play an important role in separating several unusual observations. In the cancer samples, Fusobacteria is more prominent, with unusual samples occurring at both high and low relative abundances.

There is also a second benefit. By showing how the unusual samples are positioned relative to the typical samples, the biplots offer a way to explore whether the model’s assumptions are reasonable.

This is a good example of why I find biplots useful alongside formal statistical methods. They do not replace the model, but they can reveal patterns that are difficult to appreciate from the model output alone.

References

  • Nakatsu, G. et al. (2015). Gut mucosal microbiome across stages of colorectal carcinogenesis. Nature Communications, 6, 8727.
  • Van Heerden, O., Bekker, A., Makgai, S., Otto, A. and Punzo, A. (2026). A contaminated model for overdispersed multinomial microbiome count data. arXiv:2606.02199.
NoteReproduce this analysis

The full source code is available in the website repository.

The analysis uses the development version of biplotEZ and the CDM package, which also contains the data.

devtools::install_github("MuViSU/biplotEZ")
devtools::install_github("u20439530/CDM_Package")

Once installed, the code chunks above can be used to reproduce the biplots.

item.title: When does Walmart sell? Weekly and yearly movements in 70 store departments
item.dc:creator: Raeesa
item.description:
The data

The M5 Forecasting Accuracy data were released by Walmart for a forecasting competition hosted on Kaggle. They record the number of units sold, every day, for 3049 products in 10 stores across three US states: California (CA_1 to CA_4), Texas (TX_1 to TX_3) and Wisconsin (WI_1 to WI_3). The daily record runs for 1941 days, from 29 January 2011 to 22 May 2016.

Each product belongs to one of seven departments: three food departments (FOODS_1 to FOODS_3), two hobbies departments (HOBBIES_1 and HOBBIES_2) and two household departments (HOUSEHOLD_1 and HOUSEHOLD_2). A separate calendar table says which weekday and month each of the 1941 days falls on.

That is far too much for one picture: 30490 sales series of 1941 days each. A biplot needs a modest table of rows and columns, so the first job is to decide what a row should be and what a column should be.

The question

Shops have certain movements. Weekends are busier than weekdays and some goods sell in December that nobody buys in June. The question we ask is whether every part of Walmart shares the same movement or whether some stores and some departments march to their own beat. Specifically:

  • Do the three states differ in when during the week they sell?
  • Do the seven departments differ in when during the year they sell?

Preparing the data

We chose the store department as the row: one row for each of the 10 stores crossed with the 7 departments, giving 70 rows. Each row pools all the products in that department of that store.

For the columns we want a measure of movement, not of size. FOODS_3 sells more in a day than HOBBIES_2 sells in a month and if we used raw unit counts the picture would only show that food outsells hobbies. So for each store department we computed its average daily sales on, say, Saturday, and divided by its average daily sales across all days. A value of 1.2 means Saturdays run 20 percent above that store department’s own average and 0.8 means 20 percent below. Finally we took the logarithm, which makes “20 percent above” and “20 percent below” equally far from zero. These are the numbers the biplot axes are calibrated in.

This gives two tables with the same 70 rows:

  • a weekday panel with 7 columns, Monday to Sunday, and
  • a month panel with 12 columns, January to December.

Christmas Day was dropped before averaging because every store is closed and all sales are zero. The code below shows how the panels were built from the raw Kaggle files. It is not run on this page because the raw data are close to half a gigabyte, but the two finished panels are saved next to this post as small CSV files.

Show the R code 
library(data.table)

sales <- fread("data/sales_train_evaluation.csv")
cal   <- fread("data/calendar.csv")
cal[, date := as.IDate(date)][, mday := mday(date)]

id_cols  <- c("id", "item_id", "dept_id", "cat_id", "store_id", "state_id")
day_cols <- grep("^d_", names(sales), value = TRUE)

# Reshape one store to long format (one row per product per day),
# attach the calendar and drop Christmas Day
long_store <- function(s) {
  l <- melt(sales[store_id == s], id.vars = id_cols, measure.vars = day_cols,
            variable.name = "d", value.name = "units", variable.factor = FALSE)
  l <- cal[, .(d, weekday, month, mday)][l, on = "d"]
  l[!(month == 12L & mday == 25L)]
}

# Total units (u) and number of product-days (n) per weekday and per month
agg <- lapply(sort(unique(sales$store_id)), function(s) {
  l <- long_store(s)
  list(wd = l[, .(u = sum(units), n = .N), by = .(store_id, dept_id, weekday)],
       mo = l[, .(u = sum(units), n = .N), by = .(store_id, dept_id, month)])
})
wd <- rbindlist(lapply(agg, `[[`, "wd"))
mo <- rbindlist(lapply(agg, `[[`, "mo"))

# Log ratio of the weekday's (or month's) daily rate to the store
# department's overall daily rate
to_panel <- function(x, key) {
  base <- x[, .(m = sum(u) / sum(n)), by = .(store_id, dept_id)]
  x <- merge(x, base, by = c("store_id", "dept_id"))
  x[, z := log((u / n) / m)]
  dcast(x, store_id + dept_id ~ get(key), value.var = "z")
}
weekday_panel <- to_panel(wd, "weekday")
month_panel   <- to_panel(mo, "month")
Show the R code 
# Development version of biplotEZ, installed from GitHub with
#   remotes::install_github("MuViSU/biplotEZ")
library(biplotEZ)

weekday <- read.csv("weekday_panel.csv")
month   <- read.csv("month_panel.csv")

# The 7 (or 12) movement columns become the biplot variables
W <- as.matrix(weekday[, c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
                           "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")])
M <- as.matrix(month[, month.abb])
rownames(W) <- rownames(M) <- paste(weekday$store_id, weekday$dept_id, sep = ":")

state_cols <- c(CA = "#2A6FD6", TX = "#3FAF3A", WI = "#E8891C")

The columns are already on a common scale (all are log ratios to the row’s own average), so the biplots below are centred but not standardised. Standardising would inflate the quiet months to the same importance as the busy ones, which is exactly the information we want to keep.

The weekly movement

Show the R code 
biplot(W, center = TRUE, scaled = FALSE) |>
  PCA(group.aes = weekday$state) |>
  samples(col = state_cols, pch = 16) |>
  alpha.bags(col = state_cols) |>
  axes(col = "grey35", label.cex = 0.75, ticks = 5) |>
  plot()

This two-dimensional picture reproduces 92 percent of the variation in the seven-column table, so it is a good summary.

Read the axes first. Saturday and Sunday point to the left and Monday to Thursday point to the right, with Friday pointing down between them. The tick marks on the Saturday axis reach 0.4 and beyond; a log ratio of 0.4 is about 50 percent above the store department’s average day. On the Tuesday to Thursday side the ticks are negative. So every store department sells more on the weekend, which is no surprise. The biplot is centred, so what the spread of points shows is how each store department departs from that shared pattern.

The states do not have the same weekend. The Wisconsin bag sits low in the picture, pulled along the Saturday and Friday axes. The California bag stretches up and to the left, along the Sunday axis and Texas sits between them. Projecting the points onto the axes confirms it: in Wisconsin the Friday lift is positive and the Sunday lift is less than half of California’s, while California’s peak day is Sunday. In simple terms, Wisconsin’s weekend shopping starts on Friday and peaks on Saturday and California’s peaks on Sunday. Texas is in between.

Show the R code 
biplot(W, center = TRUE, scaled = FALSE) |>
  PCA(group.aes = weekday$dept_id) |>
  samples(pch = 16) |>
  alpha.bags() |>
  axes(col = "grey35", label.cex = 0.75, ticks = 5) |>
  plot()

Departments differ less than states do. Colouring the same points by department gives bags that overlap much more, which says that where a department is matters more for its weekly movement than what it sells. Still, two departments stand out. HOBBIES_2 (magenta) hugs the right side of the picture near the weekday axes: its weekend lift is the smallest of any department, only around 10 percent above its average day. HOUSEHOLD_1 (black) reaches furthest to the left: household goods have the biggest weekend swing, with Saturdays around 25 percent above average and midweek days around 15 percent below. FOODS_2 (green) sits highest in the picture because its lift carries over into Monday, the only department for which Monday is an above-average day.

The yearly movement

Show the R code 
biplot(M, center = TRUE, scaled = FALSE) |>
  PCA(group.aes = month$dept_id) |>
  samples(pch = 16) |>
  alpha.bags() |>
  axes(col = "grey35", label.cex = 0.75, ticks = 5) |>
  plot()

The month picture explains 75 percent of the variation, less than the weekday picture and one glance shows why: most of that variation belongs to a single department.

One department has a season. The HOBBIES_2 bag sits far to the left, alone, in the direction of the October, November and December axes and directly away from June and July. Reading off the calibrations, an average HOBBIES_2 department sells about 40 percent more per day in October than in a typical month and about 20 percent more in December, but roughly 20 to 25 percent less in June and July. The other six departments crowd together near the origin, which means their sales barely change from month to month. Whatever HOBBIES_2 contains, it is the seasonal, run-up-to-the-holidays part of the shop.

Not every month is worth an axis. biplotEZ reports how well each axis is represented in the picture. October scores 0.98 and June to August all score above 0.85, so the picture reproduces those months well. May scores 0.01: the May axis is drawn but is essentially useless, because May is the one month in which nothing distinguishes one store department from another.

A few individual outliers. Away from the HOBBIES_2 cluster, the point that strays furthest is FOODS_2 in store WI_1, up and to the left, away from the June to August axes and towards January. It sells about 20 percent more in January and 20 percent less in June to August than its average, a winter pattern that none of the other food departments share. TX_3’s FOODS_1 department shows a milder version of the same thing.

Show the R code 
biplot(M, center = TRUE, scaled = FALSE) |>
  PCA(group.aes = month$state) |>
  samples(col = state_cols, pch = 16) |>
  alpha.bags(col = state_cols) |>
  axes(col = "grey35", label.cex = 0.75, ticks = 5) |>
  plot()

Geography barely matters over the year. Coloured by state, the three bags lie almost on top of one another. Wisconsin’s bag reaches a little further towards February and March and a little less towards July, so its stores are slightly quieter in summer, but this is a small effect next to the weekday differences. The yearly movement is set by the goods on the shelf and the weekly movement by where the shelf stands.

Take-aways

  • Everyone sells more on the weekend, but the states disagree on which day is the weekend: Saturday in Wisconsin, Sunday in California, with Texas in between.
  • What a department sells barely changes its weekly movement, except that household goods have the biggest weekend swing and HOBBIES_2 the smallest.
  • Over the year the roles reverse. The state makes almost no difference, while one department, HOBBIES_2, has a strong October to December season that no other department shares.
  • Expressing every cell as a log ratio to its own average is what made this possible. It removed the enormous differences in volume between departments and left only the shape of the movement, which is what the question was about.
NoteReproduce this post

This post uses the development version of biplotEZ from GitHub. Install it with remotes::install_github("MuViSU/biplotEZ") and install.packages("geometry") for the alpha bags, then run the code chunks above. The two panel files weekday_panel.csv and month_panel.csv sit next to this post. To rebuild them from the raw Kaggle data, download the M5 Forecasting Accuracy files from Kaggle into a data/ folder and run the aggregation chunk, which needs the data.table package.

item.title: What makes a red wine score well?
item.dc:creator: Raeesa and Claude
item.description:
The data

The wine quality data set was collected by Cortez and colleagues in 2009. It records eleven physicochemical measurements for 1 599 red vinho verde wines from the north of Portugal, such as acidity, sugar, alcohol and sulphur dioxide, together with a quality score from 0 to 10 awarded by a panel of tasters.

Each row is one wine. The eleven measurements are the variables we will draw as axes. The quality score is used only to colour the points, so we can see whether chemistry and taste agree.

The question

Wine chemistry is measured in a lab. Wine quality is judged by people. Do the wines that people like share a chemical profile, and if so, which measurements matter?

The biplot

Show the R code 
# Development version of biplotEZ, installed from GitHub with
#   remotes::install_github("MuViSU/biplotEZ")
# It draws with ggplot2, so install.packages("ggplot2") if needed.
library(biplotEZ)

wine <- read.csv("winequality-red.csv", sep = ";")

# Group wines into three quality bands so the colouring is easy to read
wine$band <- cut(wine$quality,
                 breaks = c(0, 5, 6, 10),
                 labels = c("Low (3-5)", "Medium (6)", "High (7-8)"))

# Tidy the variable names for the plot
names(wine) <- gsub("\\.", " ", names(wine))
Show the R code 
biplot(wine[, 1:11], group.aes = wine$band, scaled = TRUE) |>
  PCA() |>
  samples(col = c("#E8891C", "#2A6FD6", "#3FAF3A"), pch = 16, opacity = 0.6) |>
  axes(col = "grey35", label.cex = 0.75) |>
  plot()

What the picture tells us

Because the eleven measurements are on very different scales (alcohol in percent, sulphur dioxide in milligrams per litre), each variable was standardised before the biplot was built. The plot then shows the two directions in which the wines vary most.

Axes that point the same way measure the same thing. Fixed acidity and citric acid run almost parallel, and pH points the opposite way. That is the chemistry being explained: more acid means lower pH. Density and chlorides also travel together, pointing away from alcohol, because alcohol is lighter than water. Similarly, free and total sulphur dioxide point together because one is a component of the other.

High-scoring wines sit on one side. The green points drift towards the alcohol axis and away from the volatile acidity axis. Volatile acidity is essentially vinegar, so wines with more of it score lower, while wines with more alcohol and more sulphates tend to score higher. The low-scoring orange points lean the other way.

Chemistry only partly explains taste. The bands overlap heavily. Chemistry pushes a wine in a direction, but the tasting panel clearly responds to things the lab does not measure.

Take-aways

  • Alcohol and sulphates are associated with higher scores; volatile acidity with lower scores.
  • Several measurements are near duplicates of each other, so the eleven variables carry far fewer than eleven separate pieces of information.
  • A biplot puts all of this in one picture: the groupings of wines, the relationships between measurements, and the link between the two.
NoteReproduce this post

This post uses the development version of biplotEZ from GitHub. Install it with remotes::install_github("MuViSU/biplotEZ"), then run the code chunks above. The data file winequality-red.csv sits next to this post and was downloaded from the UCI Machine Learning Repository.
